arXiv:2608.21704v1 [math.AP] 22 Aug 2026

Local Well-Posedness of the Inviscid Shallow Water Equations with Surface Tension

Xin Liu Xin Liu Department of Mathematics, Texas A$M University, College Station, TX, 77843, USA. Email address: xliu23@tamu.edu and Bingheng Yang∗ Bingheng Yang Department of Mathematics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, 77843, USA. Email address: bhyang@tamu.edu
Date: August 22, 2026
Abstract.

We show that the inviscid shallow water equations with gravity and surface tension are locally well-posed in dimensions one and two. In contrast to previous works by Benzoni-Gavage, Danchin, and Descombes [9, 10], we work only in the real-valued phase space and make use of the symmetry of the system. Our alternative proof for local well-posedness sheds some light on the symmetric structure of the shallow water system and can be used for further study, including designing numerical scheme, dispersion estimate, etc.

Keyboards: Euler-Korteweg, shallow water equations, surface tension, local well-posedness, symmetric systems.

MSC2020: 35Q31, 35Q35, 76N10, 76B15, 76B45

1. Introduction

We consider the system,

(1.1a) ∂th+div⁡(h​u)\displaystyle\partial_{t}h+\Div(hu) =0\displaystyle=0\quad inℝn,\displaystyle\text{in}\quad\mathbb{R}^{n},
(1.1b) ∂tu+u⋅∇u+∇h−∇Δh\displaystyle\partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla h-\nabla\Delta h =0\displaystyle=0\quad inℝn,\displaystyle\text{in}\quad\mathbb{R}^{n},
(1.1c) (h,u)|t=0\displaystyle(h,u)|_{t=0} =(h0,u0),\displaystyle=(h_{0},u_{0}),

in dimensions n=1,2n=1,2. We can view (1.1) as a model for shallow water equations with surface tension. Here h>0h>0 denotes the height, u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denotes the velocity of the water wave, the pressure term ∇h\nabla h denotes the effect of gravity, and the third order term −∇Δh-\nabla\Delta h arises from surface tension. Physically, (1.1a) and (1.1b) stand for the conservation of mass and momentum, respectively. The shallow water equations (1.1) were formally derived from the free boundary problem for the incompressible water wave equations by the first author and his collaborators in [29], and were also previously known in the review article [13] and the monograph [15]. As a shallow water model, the validity of (1.1) was justified by Bresch and Noble in [14] in some scales.

Remark 1.1.

For n≥3n\geq 3, one should interpret (1.1) as a special case of the Euler–Korteweg system [10, 7, 11], which models a fluid with quantum effects. See Section 7 for our remark about the irrotation flows in nn dimension.

1.1. Main result

Our goal is to prove local well-posedness for (1.1). We note that the cases of n=1n=1 and n=2n=2 admit fundamentally different structures. Therefore, we will treat them separately.

In the case of n=1n=1, system (1.1) is reduced to the following:

(1.2a) ∂th+∂x(h​u)\displaystyle\partial_{t}h+\partial_{x}(hu) =0\displaystyle=0\quad inℝ,\displaystyle\text{in}\quad\mathbb{R},
(1.2b) ∂tu+u​∂xu+∂xh−∂x3h\displaystyle\partial_{t}u+u\partial_{x}u+\partial_{x}h-\partial_{x}^{3}h =0\displaystyle=0\quad inℝ,\displaystyle\text{in}\quad\mathbb{R},
(1.2c) (h,u)|t=0\displaystyle(h,u)|_{t=0} =(h0,u0).\displaystyle=(h_{0},u_{0}).
Theorem 1.2.

Consider initial data (h0,u0)(h_{0},u_{0}) for system (1.2), with

(1.3) 0<h¯:=infxh0​(x)<1<h¯:=supxh0​(x)<∞,0<\underline{h}:=\inf_{x}h_{0}(x)<1<\overline{h}:=\sup_{x}h_{0}(x)<\infty,

and

(1.4) h0−1∈H3​(ℝ),u0∈H2​(ℝ).h_{0}-1\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R}),\quad u_{0}\in H^{2}(\mathbb{R}).

Then there exists T∈(0,∞)T\in(0,\infty), depending only on the initial data, such that there exists a unique solution (h−1,u)∈L∞​([0,T],H3​(ℝ))×L∞​([0,T],H2​(ℝ))(h-1,u)\in L^{\infty}([0,T];H^{3}(\mathbb{R}))\times L^{\infty}([0,T];H^{2}(\mathbb{R})) to system (1.2), with

(1.5) sup0≤t≤T∑0≤j≤2∥∂xj(h(t)−1),∂xju(t),∂xj+1h(t)∥L2<C<∞,\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\sum_{0\leq j\leq 2}\|\partial_{x}^{j}(h(t)-1),\partial_{x}^{j}u(t),\partial_{x}^{j+1}h(t)\|_{L^{2}}<C<\infty,

for some constant C∈(0,∞)C\in(0,\infty) depending only on the initial data.

Meanwhile, in the case of n=2n=2, we will show

Theorem 1.3.

Consider initial data (h0,u0)(h_{0},u_{0}) for system (1.1), with

(1.6) 0<h¯:=infxh0​(x)<1<h¯:=supxh0​(x)<∞,0<\underline{h}:=\inf_{x}h_{0}(x)<1<\overline{h}:=\sup_{x}h_{0}(x)<\infty,

and with regularity

(1.7) h0−1∈H7​(ℝ),u0∈H6​(ℝ2).h_{0}-1\in H^{7}(\mathbb{R}),\quad u_{0}\in H^{6}(\mathbb{R}^{2}).

Then there exists T∈(0,∞)T\in(0,\infty) depending only initial data, such that there exists a unique solution (h−1,u)∈L∞​([0,T],H4​(ℝ))×L∞​([0,T],H3​(ℝ2))(h-1,u)\in L^{\infty}([0,T];H^{4}(\mathbb{R}))\times L^{\infty}([0,T];H^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{2})) to system (1.1), with

(1.8) sup0≤t≤T∑0≤j≤3∥∇j(h(t)−1),∇ju(t),∇j+1h(t)∥L2<C<∞,\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\sum_{0\leq j\leq 3}\|\nabla^{j}(h(t)-1),\nabla^{j}u(t),\nabla^{j+1}h(t)\|_{L^{2}}<C<\infty,

for some constant C∈(0,∞)C\in(0,\infty) depending only on the initial data.

To prove Theorems 1.2 and 1.3, we will make use of the symmetric structure of system (1.1), which can be seen via the momentum variable m:=h​u.m:=hu. Indeed, one can write down the following equivalent system of the shallow water equations using (h,m)(h,m):

(1.9a) ∂th+div⁡m\displaystyle\partial_{t}h+\Div m =0,\displaystyle=0,
(1.9b) 1h∂tm+mh2⋅∇m+mh2divm+∇h−∇Δh\displaystyle\frac{1}{h}\partial_{t}m+\frac{m}{h^{2}}\cdot\nabla m+\frac{m}{h^{2}}\Div m+\nabla h-\nabla\Delta h =(m⋅∇)hh3​m,\displaystyle=\frac{(m\cdot\nabla)h}{h^{3}}m,
(1.9c) ∂t∇h+∇div⁡m\displaystyle\partial_{t}\nabla h+\nabla\Div m =0.\displaystyle=0.

To explain the idea, in the case of n=1n=1, i.e., in one spatial dimension, let U:=(h−1,m,∂xh)⊤∈ℝ3U:=(h-1,m,\partial_{x}h)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. One can write system (1.2) (or equivalently, system (1.9)) as

(1.10a) (10001h0001)​∂tU+(01012​mh20000)​∂xU+(00000−1010)​∂x2U=(0m2h3​∂xh0),\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&\frac{1}{h}&0\\ 0&0&1\\ \end{pmatrix}\partial_{t}U+\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 1&\frac{2m}{h^{2}}&0\\ 0&0&0\\ \end{pmatrix}\partial_{x}U+\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\ 0&0&-1\\ 0&1&0\\ \end{pmatrix}\partial_{x}^{2}U=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ \frac{m^{2}}{h^{3}}\partial_{x}h\\ 0\\ \end{pmatrix},
(1.10b) U⁡(0,x)=(h0−1,m0,∂xh0).\displaystyle U(0,x)=(h_{0}-1,m_{0},\partial_{x}h_{0}).

One can see that system (1.10) resembles a symmetric hyperbolic system, with additional second order terms. In particular, the associated linear operator generates a bounded group, and therefore there is no loss of regularity; see Lemma 2.2, below. Due to this symmetry, the local well-posedness of the generalized system (2.5) follows easily from the method of vanishing viscosity. We refer to Section 3 for the complete argument. At last, in Section 4, we show the well-posedness of system (1.10) (or equivalently, system (1.2)) using an approximating argument.

However, in dimension two, the symmetric structure of the shallow water system (1.1) differs from that in (1.10). Indeed, only the acoustic component of the flow admits a symmetric structure, while the vorticity component of the flow is transported. See Section 5 for the detailed formulation of n=2n=2, as well as the a priori estimates for the 2d system (5.12). In Section 6 we explain why the approximating argument in Section 4 cannot be directly applied to the 2d case without additional regularity assumptions. Finally, in Section 7, we remark about a result for irrotational flows in dimensions ≥3\geq 3.

1.2. Background and literature on inviscid water waves with gravity and surface tension

For inviscid shallow water equations without surface tension, or for viscous shallow water equations with surface tension, we refer the reader to Bresch’s book [15], Lannes’ works [27, 28] and the review article by Bresch–Desjardins–Métivier [13] for an extensive overview on the mathematical properties of shallow water models in the absence/presence of boundary. In particular, Bresch and Noble in [14] rigorously justified the validity of (1.1) in smooth function spaces.

Much more mathematical studies on inviscid water waves are available without the assumption of shallowness. Here we highlight the following works: Wu [35, 36, 33, 34], Coutand–Shkoller [19], Alazard–Burq–Zuily [2, 4, 3] and Deng–Ionescu–Pausader–Pusateri [24, 25, 26, 20] managed to show local and global well-posedness of incompressible irrotational water waves with or without surface tension using various methods, whereas Castro–Córdoba–Fefferman–Gancedo–Gómez-Serrano [17, 16] investigated the finite-time formation of splash singularities. Finally, we note that Ambrose–Masmoudi [5, 6] and Agrawal [1] investigated the zero surface tension limit problem.

We remark here that Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 corresponds to the K=1K=1 case for the Euler–Korteweg system in [10, Theorem 1.1]. The proof in [10] relies on finding the good variable

w:=∇hh,w:=\frac{\nabla h}{\sqrt{h}},

then complexifying the equations and performing rather involved weighted energy estimates. Moreover, the argument in [10] requires a vanishing viscosity argument using the hyperdissipative term −ε​Δ2-\varepsilon\Delta^{2}, for which uniform-in-ε\varepsilon estimates are more difficult to establish. We provide a shorter and more physically intuitive proof based on another good variable (5.16), which in turn gives more insights to the hidden symmetric structure of (1.1). In addition, we believe that our approach based on (almost) symmetric systems can be useful for further numerical studies of shallow water waves. See for instance [12, 21, 8, 22, 23, 30, 39, 37, 38] for numerical studies of shallow water models and of the Euler–Korteweg system.

4. Well-posedness of the 1d shallow water system (2.1)

We now are ready to establish well-posedness system (2.1) for initial data with regularity (h0−1,m0)∈H3​(ℝ)×H2​(ℝ)(h_{0}-1,m_{0})\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{2}(\mathbb{R}). To do so, we need elliptic estimates and energy estimates for the original shallow water system (2.1). We emphasize that the elliptic estimates are not available for the generalized system (2.5); see Remark 4.2, below.

4.1. Elliptic estimates

We define the evolutionary energy

(4.1) ℱ(t):=∑0≤i≤1∥∂ti(h−1),∂timh,∂ti∂xh∥L22,\mathcal{F}(t):=\sum_{0\leq i\leq 1}\|\partial_{t}^{i}(h-1),\frac{\partial_{t}^{i}m}{\sqrt{h}},\partial_{t}^{i}\partial_{x}h\|_{L^{2}}^{2},

(4.2) 𝔉(t):=∑0≤j≤2∥∂xj(h−1),∂xjmh,∂xj∂xh∥L22.\mathfrak{F}(t):=\sum_{0\leq j\leq 2}\|\partial_{x}^{j}(h-1),\frac{\partial_{x}^{j}m}{\sqrt{h}},\partial_{x}^{j}\partial_{x}h\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.

Similar to (2.8), we make the a priori assumption for hh:

(4.3) 0<12​h¯≤infx,th⁡(x,t)≤supx,th⁡(x,t)≤2​h¯.0<\frac{1}{2}\underline{h}\leq\inf_{x,t}h(x,t)\leq\sup_{x,t}h(x,t)\leq 2\overline{h}.

Under the a priori assumption 4.3, there exists a positive polynomial 𝒢1\mathcal{G}_{1} such that

Proof.

For the original system (2.1), we have

(4.5) ‖∂xm‖L2=‖∂th‖L2,\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}m\|_{L^{2}}=\|\partial_{t}h\|_{L^{2}},
(4.6) ‖∂x2m‖L2=‖∂t∂xh‖L2.\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}^{2}m\|_{L^{2}}=\|\partial_{t}\partial_{x}h\|_{L^{2}}.

At the same time, applying integration by parts, one has that

(4.7) ∥∂x3h∥L22+∥∂xh∥L22+2∥∂x2h∥L22=∥−∂x3h+∂xh∥L22=‖1h​∂tm+2​m​∂xmh2−m2​∂xhh3‖L22≲‖∂tm‖L22+‖m‖H14+‖m‖H14​‖∂xh‖L22,\begin{gathered}\|\partial_{x}^{3}h\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\partial_{x}h\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+2\|\partial_{x}^{2}h\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=\|-\partial_{x}^{3}h+\partial_{x}h\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\\ =\|\frac{1}{h}\partial_{t}m+\frac{2m\partial_{x}m}{h^{2}}-\frac{m^{2}\partial_{x}h}{h^{3}}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim\|\partial_{t}m\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|m\|_{H^{1}}^{4}+\|m\|_{H^{1}}^{4}\|\partial_{x}h\|_{L^{2}}^{2},\end{gathered}

where we have applied (4.3). This finishes the proof of (4.4).

∎

Remark 4.2.

Lemma 4.1 does not hold for the generalized system (2.5). Indeed, in the (η−1,ω,ϕ)(\eta-1,\omega,\phi)-variable, the corresponding estimate (4.7) becomes

∥−∂x2ϕ+∂xh∥L22≲∥∂tω∥L22+∥ω∥H14+∥ω∥H12∥ϕ∥L2.\|-\partial_{x}^{2}\phi+\partial_{x}h\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim\|\partial_{t}\omega\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\omega\|_{H^{1}}^{4}+\|\omega\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\|\phi\|_{L^{2}}.

In particular, since ϕ≠∂xh\phi\neq\partial_{x}h in general, one cannot obtain the higher order regularity of hh from the left hand side of the above estimate.

By making use of the elliptic estimate (4.4) for the shallow water system (2.1), we will be able to obtain sharper regularity for the solutions.

For the shallow water system (2.1), we have the following analog to Lemma 2.2:

(4.9) A0​(U)​∂tUt+A1​(U)​∂xUt+A2​∂x2Ut=𝔊t,A_{0}(U)\partial_{t}U_{t}+A_{1}(U)\partial_{x}U_{t}+A_{2}\partial_{x}^{2}U_{t}=\mathfrak{G}_{t},

4.3. Proof of Theorem 1.2

By taking η=h\eta=h, ω=m\omega=m, and ϕ=∂xh\phi=\partial_{x}h in system (2.5), for (h0−1,m0)∈H5​(ℝ)×H4​(ℝ)(h_{0}-1,m_{0})\in H^{5}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{4}(\mathbb{R}), Proposition 2.4 implies that there exists a unique solution (h−1,m)∈H3​(ℝ)×H2​(ℝ)(h-1,m)\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{2}(\mathbb{R}) to the shallow water system (2.1).

In general, for (h0−1,m0)∈H3​(ℝ)×H2​(ℝ)(h_{0}-1,m_{0})\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{2}(\mathbb{R}), one chooses a sequence of initial data (hk,0−1,mk,0)∈H5​(ℝ)×H4​(ℝ)(h_{k,0}-1,m_{k,0})\in H^{5}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{4}(\mathbb{R}), k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, such that

(4.11) hk,0−1\displaystyle h_{k,0}-1 →h0−1\displaystyle\rightarrow h_{0}-1 in​H3​(ℝ),\displaystyle\text{in}\ H^{3}(\mathbb{R}),
mk,0\displaystyle m_{k,0} →m0\displaystyle\rightarrow m_{0} in​H2​(ℝ),\displaystyle\text{in}\ H^{2}(\mathbb{R}),

and the initial data

(4.12) Vk,0:=(hk,0−1mk,0∂xhk,0)∈H3​(ℝ)×H4​(ℝ)×H4​(ℝ).V_{k,0}:=\begin{pmatrix}h_{k,0}-1\\ m_{k,0}\\ \partial_{x}h_{k,0}\end{pmatrix}\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{4}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{4}(\mathbb{R}).

The well-posedness theory of the generalized system (2.5) implies that for each fixed k=1,2,…k=1,2,\ldots, there exists Tk∈(0,∞)T_{k}\in(0,\infty) such that we have a unique solution Vk:=(hk−1,mk,ϕk)⊤V_{k}:=(h_{k}-1,m_{k},\phi_{k})^{\top}. In particular, (hk−1,mk)(h_{k}-1,m_{k}) is a solution to the shallow water system (2.1).

Applying Proposition 4.4 and Lemma 4.1, one obtains the following estimate:

(4.13) sup0≤t≤𝔗′{∥hk(t)−1∥H32+∥mk(t)∥H22+∥hk(t)−1,∂thk(t)∥H12+∥mk(t),∂tm(t)∥L22}≲∥∂tmk,0,mk,0∥L22+∥∂thk,0,hk,0−1∥H12≲∥hk,0−1∥H32+∥mk,0∥H22,\begin{gathered}\sup_{0\leq t\leq\mathfrak{T}^{\prime}}\bigl\{\|h_{k}(t)-1\|_{H^{3}}^{2}+\|m_{k}(t)\|_{H^{2}}^{2}+\|h_{k}(t)-1,\partial_{t}h_{k}(t)\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|m_{k}(t),\partial_{t}m(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigr\}\\ \lesssim\|\partial_{t}m_{k,0},m_{k,0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\partial_{t}h_{k,0},h_{k,0}-1\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\lesssim\|h_{k,0}-1\|_{H^{3}}^{2}+\|m_{k,0}\|_{H^{2}}^{2},\end{gathered}

for some sufficiently short time 𝔗′>0\mathfrak{T}^{\prime}>0 independent of kk. The last inequality follows from directly using the equations (2.1) to obtain the initial data for the time derivatives, similar to (2.11). Therefore, by the convergence (4.11) and the bound (4.13), passing the limit k→∞k\rightarrow\infty, one obtains the unique solution (h−1,m)∈L∞​([0,𝔗′],H3​(ℝ))×L∞​([0,𝔗′],H2​(ℝ))(h-1,m)\in L^{\infty}([0,\mathfrak{T}^{\prime}];H^{3}(\mathbb{R}))\times L^{\infty}([0,\mathfrak{T}^{\prime}];H^{2}(\mathbb{R})) to the shallow water system (2.1). The uniqueness and continuous dependence on the initial data follow with arguments similar to those in Section 3.3. This concludes the proof of Theorem 1.2 after recalling u=mhu=\frac{m}{h}.

5. A priori estimate for two dimensional flow

5.1. Symmetric reformulation

We will turn our focus to the case of multi-dimensions in system (1.1). In this section, we consider the case when n=2n=2, i.e., the two dimensional flow. To be more precise, we will only establish the a priori estimate using the symmetric structure. The local well-posedness follows via similar arguments as in Sections 3–4.

For ℝ2={(x1,x2)}\mathbb{R}^{2}=\{(x_{1},x_{2})\}, we write, for j=1,2j=1,2,

(5.1) ∂j:=∂xj.\partial_{j}:=\partial_{x_{j}}.

We write, for any vector field v=(v1,v2)⊤v=(v_{1},v_{2})^{\top},

v⟂:=(−v2v1)=Jv,∇⟂:=(−∂2∂1)=J∇,v^{\perp}:=\begin{pmatrix}-v_{2}\\ v_{1}\end{pmatrix}=Jv,\quad\nabla^{\perp}:=\begin{pmatrix}-\partial_{2}\\ \partial_{1}\\ \end{pmatrix}=J\nabla,

where

(5.2) J:=(0−110),J:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix},

and we consider the 2d flow with the non-degenerate condition

(5.3) 0<12​h¯≤infx,th⁡(x,t)≤supx,th⁡(x,t)≤2​h¯<∞.0<\frac{1}{2}\underline{h}\leq\inf_{x,t}h(x,t)\leq\sup_{x,t}h(x,t)\leq 2\overline{h}<\infty.

Similarly as before, consider the momentum variable m=(m1,m2)⊤:=h​u=h​(u1,u2)⊤m=(m_{1},m_{2})^{\top}:=hu=h(u_{1},u_{2})^{\top}. 6. Remark on the regularity (1.7) for 2-dimensional flows

The purpose of Section 6 is to demonstrate the optimal regularity argument in Section 4 fails in dimension two. Namely, we cannot relax the regularity of the initial data from (h0−1,u0)∈H7​(ℝ)×H6​(ℝ2)(h_{0}-1,u_{0})\in H^{7}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{6}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) to (h0−1,u0)∈H4​(ℝ)×H3​(ℝ2)(h_{0}-1,u_{0})\in H^{4}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{2}). The integer Sobolev index corresponding to n=2n=2 is s=3s=3: The corresponding evolution energy and elliptic energy are

(6.1) ℱbad(t):=∑0≤i≤1,0≤i+|α|≤2∥∂ti∂α(h−1),∂ti∂αmh,∂ti∂α∇h∥L22,\mathcal{F}_{\text{bad}}(t):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq i\leq 1,\\ 0\leq i+|\alpha|\leq 2\end{subarray}}\|\partial_{t}^{i}\partial^{\alpha}(h-1),\frac{\partial_{t}^{i}\partial^{\alpha}m}{\sqrt{h}},\partial_{t}^{i}\partial^{\alpha}\nabla h\|_{L^{2}}^{2},

and

(6.2) 𝔉bad(t):=∑0≤|α|≤3∥∂α(h−1),∂αmh,∂α∇h∥L22,\mathfrak{F}_{\text{bad}}(t):=\sum_{0\leq|\alpha|\leq 3}\|\partial^{\alpha}(h-1),\frac{\partial^{\alpha}m}{\sqrt{h}},\partial^{\alpha}\nabla h\|_{L^{2}}^{2},

respectively. To integrate by parts in the energy estimates, one needs to compute, for |α|=1|\alpha|=1,

(6.3) ∂t∂α(1h​∂tm)​∂t∂αm=[∂α(1h)⏟∈L∞​∂t2m]​∂t∂αm⏟∈L2+⋯.\partial_{t}\partial^{\alpha}\left(\frac{1}{h}\partial_{t}m\right)\partial_{t}\partial^{\alpha}m=[\underbrace{\partial^{\alpha}\left(\frac{1}{h}\right)}_{\in L^{\infty}}\boxed{\partial_{t}^{2}m}]\underbrace{\partial_{t}\partial^{\alpha}m}_{\in L^{2}}+\cdots.

We require ∂t2m∈Lx2\partial_{t}^{2}m\in L_{x}^{2}: A direct calculation using (1.9b) gives

(6.4) 1h∂t2m+⋯=∂t∇Δh+⋯.\displaystyle\frac{1}{h}{\partial_{t}^{2}m}+\cdots={\partial_{t}\nabla\Delta h}+\cdots.

However, the term ∂t∇Δh\partial_{t}\nabla\Delta h is not in the evolution energy (6.1). Consequently, ℱbad\mathcal{F}_{\text{bad}} and 𝔉bad\mathfrak{F}_{\text{bad}} cannot satisfy an inequality of the form (4.4) due to a loss of regularity. Hence, we conclude that it is not possible to loosen the regularity (1.7) to the optimal regularity (h0−1,m0)∈H4​(ℝ)×H3​(ℝ2)(h_{0}-1,m_{0})\in H^{4}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) without imposing additional regularity assumptions on m0m_{0}.

Remark 6.1.

We do not try to optimize the regularity as in Section 4 for dimensional higher than 11 hereafter.

7. nn-dimensional irrotational flows, n≥3n\geq 3

For flows in dimensions 33 or larger, one can still write down the system (1.1) as a sum of the symmetric and non-symmetric parts as in (5.12). However, the corresponding vorticity does not satisfy a transport equation similar to (5.15).

To be more precise, let Ji​j,Ii​j∈ℝn×nJ_{ij},I_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, 1≤i,j≤n1\leq i,j\leq n, be matrices defined by

(7.1) (Ji​j)l​k:=−δl​i​δk​j+δk​i​δl​j,(Ii​j)l​k:=δl​i​δk​j+δk​i​δl​j.(J_{ij})_{lk}:=-\delta_{li}\delta_{kj}+\delta_{ki}\delta_{lj},\qquad(I_{ij})_{lk}:=\delta_{li}\delta_{kj}+\delta_{ki}\delta_{lj}.

In analogy to (5.6), we focus on the term

(7.2) K:=mh2⋅∇m+mh2​div⁡m=∑i=1nBi​∂im,K:=\frac{m}{h^{2}}\cdot\nabla m+\frac{m}{h^{2}}\Div m=\sum_{i=1}^{n}B_{i}\partial_{i}m,

where

(7.3) (Bi)l​k=mih2​δl​k+mlh2​δk​i.(B_{i})_{lk}=\frac{m_{i}}{h^{2}}\delta_{lk}+\frac{m_{l}}{h^{2}}\delta_{ki}.

Then one can write

(7.4) Bi=Bi,sym+∑j=1nAi​j,B_{i}=B_{\mathrm{i,sym}}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij},

where

(7.5) Bi,sym\displaystyle B_{\mathrm{i,sym}} :=mih2​𝕀n+∑j=1nmj2​h2​Ii​j,\displaystyle:=\frac{m_{i}}{h^{2}}\mathbb{I}_{n}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{m_{j}}{2h^{2}}I_{ij},
Ai​j\displaystyle A_{ij} :=mj2​h2​Ji​j.\displaystyle:=\frac{m_{j}}{2h^{2}}J_{ij}.

Indeed,

(Ii​j+Ji​j)l​k\displaystyle(I_{ij}+J_{ij})_{lk} =2​δk​i​δl​j,\displaystyle=2\delta_{ki}\delta_{lj},
by definition, and therefore
(Bi,sym+∑j=1nAi​j)l​k\displaystyle(B_{\mathrm{i,sym}}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij})_{lk} =mih2​δl​k+∑j=1nmj2​h2​(Ii​j+Ji​j)l​k\displaystyle=\frac{m_{i}}{h^{2}}\delta_{lk}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{m_{j}}{2h^{2}}(I_{ij}+J_{ij})_{lk}
=mih2​δl​k+∑j=1nmj2​h2​2​δk​i​δl​j=mih2​δl​k+mlh2​δk​i​=(7.3)​(Bi)l​k.\displaystyle=\frac{m_{i}}{h^{2}}\delta_{lk}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{m_{j}}{2h^{2}}2\delta_{ki}\delta_{lj}=\frac{m_{i}}{h^{2}}\delta_{lk}+\frac{m_{l}}{h^{2}}\delta_{ki}\overset{\eqref{def:B-i}}{=}(B_{i})_{lk}.

Therefore, substituting (7.4) and (7.5) into (7.2) yields

(7.6) K\displaystyle K =∑i=1nBi,sym​∂im+∑i,j=1nmj2​h2​Ji​j​∂im\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}B_{\mathrm{i,sym}}\partial_{i}m+\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\frac{m_{j}}{2h^{2}}J_{ij}\partial_{i}m
=∑i=1nBi,sym∂im+∑i,j=1nmj2​h2Ji​j(∂im−∇mi)⏟=(∇skwm)i+∑i,j=1nmj2​h2Ji​j∇mi,\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}B_{\mathrm{i,sym}}\partial_{i}m+\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\frac{m_{j}}{2h^{2}}J_{ij}\underbrace{(\partial_{i}m-\nabla m_{i})}_{=(\nabla_{\mathrm{skw}}m)_{i}}+\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\frac{m_{j}}{2h^{2}}J_{ij}\nabla m_{i},

in analogy to (5.26).

Now we are ready to write the system (1.9) into symmetric form in higher dimensions. Let U:=(h−1,m,∇h)=(h−1,m1,m2,⋯,mn,∂1h,∂2h,⋯,∂nh)∈ℝ2​n+1U:=(h-1,m,\nabla h)=(h-1,m_{1},m_{2},\cdots,m_{n},\partial_{1}h,\partial_{2}h,\cdots,\partial_{n}h)\in\mathbb{R}^{2n+1}.
